newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese claim half of Zhuzhou zinc shorts covered.
newsitem.headline: Chinese claim half of Zhuzhou zinc shorts covered.

text.p: Between a half and two thirds of the Zhuzhou smelter's estimated 90,000 tonnes of short zinc positions on the London Metal Exchange (LME) have now been covered, a senior Chinese industry source said on Monday.

The source, close to government metal authorities in Beijing, told Reuters Zhuzhou is working overtime to meet its contracts, taking delivery of crude zinc to process into special high grade (SHG) that can be delivered on the LME.
He said the smelter was renegotiating long-term contracts with physical buyers so it can deliver slightly lower quality, non-LME registered high grade (HG) zinc, instead of SHG.
"A lot of end users can make do with high grade," he said, adding the Chinese HG was being offered at a discount of $100 a tonne on the LME SHG price.
Regional metal dealers said they had not heard of such deals, but ageed a discount of $100 would be a fine incentive to a buyer who did not need the purer SHG zinc.
Zinc prices are caught in a vicious cycle of fund buying and short covering that could see the price of the metal on the LME soar through $1,700 a tonne, the dealers said.
"Zinc is just crazy and it will stay crazy because of the Chinese shorts," a Singapore trader said.

Chinese smelters, including Zhuzhou, had sold more than 250,000 tonnes of zinc at around $1,100 a tonne for delivery in August and September, an executive with a Chinese state broking firm told Reuters.

"All the smelters put together would have sold more than 250,000 tonnes," he said, adding that this figure would include smelters outside the direct control of the government's China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC).
These figures inspired a wave of speculative buying late last week, which on Friday pushed the price of three-month metal to fresh seven-year highs above $1,600 a tonne.
LME cash zinc was quoted at $1,690 a tonne in early Asia trade on Monday.
Asian traders were bullish on zinc's direction, seeing the metal now caught in a fund-buying cycle that compounded the complicated fundamentals.
"You'd never have thought a year ago that we'd be looking at these prices today. I didn't think it would go over $1,450," a European trader said.
"Until the Chinese cover their shorts, it could go anywhere," he said, repeating some estimates of levels as high as $2,000 a tonne and adding: "It's ludicrous."
"It's overbought, but people are still buying. It's investor-driven," another trader in the region said.

With Chinese smelters seen having to cover their massive short positions, a great speculative opportunity had opened up for investment funds that had swept into the market on the back of the current squeeze, traders said.
LME broker firm Brandeis said in its daily review on that technically zinc's constructive close on the LME on Friday had set the scene for three-month metal to test $1,700.

The excitement caused by the zinc rally had spilled over into other metals, traders in the region said, with good prospects for copper, aluminium and nickel -- which was now looking at a target of $7,400 a tonne.
